title: Only the bird's head
hook: book three opens with the three inner limbs in three short sutras: hold the mind in one place, let it flow, then disappear into what you're seeing
carry: dharana, dhyana, samadhi: hold, flow, only the target

segments.voice: Yesterday: pratyahara. Kama brought spring to the mountain, and Shiva's eyes stayed closed: settle the mind, and the senses follow. And book two closed.

The teacher Drona sets a wooden bird high in a tree and calls his students to aim. In a story often told from the Mahabharata, he asks each one before he shoots: what do you see? One sees the tree, the branches, the sky, his brothers. Drona sends him away. Then Arjuna steps up. What do you see? The bird. Describe the bird. I see only its head. Shoot. Popular retellings make it the eye; the epic says the head. Book three of the Yoga Sutras is called Vibhuti, the book of powers. But it opens with Arjuna's kind of seeing, in three steps.
screen: `A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `ONLY ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.1: dharana, concentration, is binding the mind to one place. The classical commentary lists places: the navel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or something outside the body. Dharana comes from a root meaning to hold, the same root as dharma. You hold the mind there, the way you'd hold a cup steady. It slips. You bring it back. That's dharana. Sutra 3.2: dhyana, meditation, is when the idea of that object flows on without a break. One thread, no knots. A later image some teachers use: oil poured from one jar to another, a single unbroken stream. Sutra 3.3: samadhi, absorption, is that same flow when only the object shines, as if empty of its own form. In dhyana, there's still you, meditating on something. In samadhi, the sense of me meditating drops away. Only the bird's head. Arjuna in the story isn't thinking, I'm concentrating well. There's just the target. These aren't three separate techniques. They're one movement, deepening. Hold. Flow. Disappear into it. Hindu worship trains this every day. Before many pujas, families recite a dhyana shloka, a meditation verse that paints the god's form. One well-loved verse pictures a god clad in white, bright as the moon, with four arms; many families say it for Ganesha. The verse gives the mind one bird's head to hold. Patanjali's claim is that this can be trained, and pointed at the deepest things.
screen: `DHARANA: HOLD THE MIND IN ONE PLACE.` · `DHYANA: AN UNBROKEN FLOW.` · `SAMADHI: ONLY THE OBJECT SHINES.` · `A VERSE THAT PAINTS THE GOD'S FORM.` · then, large: `HOLD, FLOW, ONLY THE TARGET.`

segments.voice: Choose one place, the tip of the nose where the breath touches or the center of the chest, and hold the mind there; when it slips, and it will, bring it back without scolding. That's dharana. If for a few breaths it stays without your holding, notice the flow: a taste of dhyana.
Concentration. Dharana, binding the mind to one place, the first of the three inner limbs, which deepen into meditation and absorption.
Your line: dharana, dhyana, samadhi: hold, flow, only the target. Book three opens with seeing only the bird's head. Rest well.

howItsDone: In Hindu worship and meditation, practitioners often fix attention on one point, such as a sacred image, a mantra or the heart, and many begin puja with a dhyana shloka, a verse describing the deity's form; teachers describe concentration deepening into meditation and absorption over long practice.

chat.meaning: Arjuna saw only the bird's head. A dhyana shloka gives the mind one form to hold, dharana, so it can flow into meditation and, in time, absorption.

tie.story: When Drona asked his students what they saw, Arjuna said only the bird's head, and Drona told him to shoot.

notes: The bird's-eye test is widely told; whether it appears in the critical edition of the Mahabharata, and in what form, should be checked. Framed as 'a story often told from the Mahabharata'.
The oil-stream image (tailadhara) for meditation is used by later teachers (e.g. Ramanuja); not attributed to Patanjali or the Bhashya.
Dharana and dharma sharing the root dhṛ: confirm.
